question: Which AI practices does Article 5 of the AI Act prohibit?
answer_points: Prohibited: AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person's consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm (Art. 5(1)(a)).
Prohibited: AI systems that exploit vulnerabilities of persons due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation, causing significant harm (Art. 5(1)(b)).

Prohibited: AI systems that generate or manipulate intimate images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable person without their freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent (Art. 5(1)(ba)).
Prohibited: AI systems that generate or manipulate child sexual abuse material within the meaning of Directive 2011/93/EU, except where a 'without right' defence applies (Art. 5(1)(bb)).
Prohibited: social scoring systems whose score leads to detrimental treatment in unrelated contexts or that is unjustified or disproportionate (Art. 5(1)(c)).

Prohibited: AI systems predicting the risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits, except to support human assessment already based on objective and verifiable facts (Art. 5(1)(d)).
Prohibited: AI systems creating or expanding facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV (Art. 5(1)(e)).
Prohibited: emotion inference in the workplace and education institutions, except for medical or safety reasons (Art. 5(1)(f)).

Prohibited: biometric categorisation deducing race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, except for labelling/filtering of lawfully acquired datasets and law-enforcement categorisation (Art. 5(1)(g)).

Prohibited: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, unless strictly necessary for a listed objective: targeted search for victims/missing persons (h)(i), prevention of a specific substantial and imminent life/safety threat or terrorist attack (h)(ii), or localisation of suspects of Annex II offences punishable by at least four years (h)(iii) (Art. 5(1)(h)).
The prohibitions in Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb) apply only from 2 December 2026 and so not yet on the as-of date (Art. 113(a)).
notes: Framing question over Art. 5(1); one gold ref per prohibited practice. Text includes Digital Omnibus amendments (ba), (bb), (1a), (1b). (1a)-(1b) conditions on (ba)/(bb) prohibitions and Art. 5(2)-(7) procedural rules on real-time RBI summarised only where part of a practice's definition.

question: What information must the EU declaration of conformity for a high-risk AI system contain?
answer_points: The AI system name and type and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (Annex V).
The name and address of the provider or, where applicable, of the authorised representative (Annex V).
A statement that the declaration is issued under the sole responsibility of the provider (Annex V).
A statement that the system is in conformity with the AI Act and, if applicable, with other relevant Union law providing for the declaration (Annex V).
Where the system involves processing of personal data, a statement that it complies with Regulations (EU) 2016/679 and (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680 (Annex V).
References to any relevant harmonised standards or other common specification used (Annex V).
Where applicable, the name and number of the notified body, a description of the conformity assessment procedure and identification of the certificate (Annex V).
The place and date of issue, the name and function of the signatory, for whom they signed, and a signature (Annex V).
optional_points: The declaration must be translated into a language easily understood by the national competent authorities (Art. 47(2)).
notes: Eight required points, one per point of Annex V, because the question asks for the full content.

question: How does the AI Act define an "AI system"?
answer_points: An AI system is a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment (Art. 3(1)).

An AI system, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to generate outputs (predictions, content, recommendations or decisions) that can influence physical or virtual environments (Art. 3(1)).

question: Who is a "deployer" under the AI Act?
answer_points: A deployer is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity (Art. 3(4)).

question: From when do the obligations for high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III apply?
answer_points: The high-risk obligations in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3 (except Article 6(5)) apply to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027 (Art. 113(c)(i)).

question: Since when do the prohibitions in Article 5 of the AI Act apply?
answer_points: The prohibitions in Article 5 have applied since 2 February 2025 (Art. 113(a)).
The prohibitions in Article 5(1)(ba) and (bb), with Article 5(1a) and (1b), apply only from 2 December 2026 (Art. 113(a)).

question: A company uses an AI system to filter job applications before a recruiter sees them. Which risk class applies under the AI Act?
answer_points: The AI system is high-risk (Annex III, point 4(a)).

question: A bank uses an AI system to assess the creditworthiness of private customers. Is it a high-risk AI system?
answer_points: The AI system is high-risk (Annex III, point 5(b)).

question: How do Article 10 of the AI Act and Article 9 of the GDPR relate when special categories of personal data are processed to detect bias?
answer_points: Bias in training, validation and testing data must be examined, and measures taken to detect, prevent and mitigate it (Art. 10(2)(f); Art. 10(2)(g)).
The GDPR prohibits processing special categories of personal data (gdpr Art. 9(1)).

Providers of high-risk AI systems may exceptionally process such data to the extent strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, if it cannot be done with other data and all listed safeguards are met (Art. 4a(1)).
These conditions apply in addition to the GDPR (Art. 4a(1)).
notes: The exception was in Art. 10(5) before the Digital Omnibus.

question: Which rights does a person have under the AI Act and the GDPR when a decision about them is based on the output of a high-risk AI system?
answer_points: A person significantly affected, in a way they consider adverse, by a deployer's decision based on an Annex III high-risk system (except point 2) can obtain a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role and the main elements of the decision (Art. 86(1)).

For automated decision-making referred to in Article 22 GDPR, the person is entitled to meaningful information about the logic involved, the significance and the envisaged consequences (gdpr Art. 13(2)(f); gdpr Art. 14(2)(g); gdpr Art. 15(1)(h)).
Where a solely automated decision rests on a contract or explicit consent, the person can at least obtain human intervention, express their point of view and contest the decision (gdpr Art. 22(3)).

question: What is the case number of the first court ruling on the AI Act?
How many AI systems are registered in the EU database today?
Why does Article 99 of the AI Act ban chatbots?
answer_points: Article 99 regulates penalties and enforcement measures, not bans on AI systems or chatbots (Art. 99).

question: Which provisions of the GDPR were repealed by the AI Act?
answer_points: The AI Act does not affect the GDPR (Art. 2(7)).
Both regulations apply simultaneously when AI systems process personal data (Art. 2(7)).
The AI Act adds AI-specific requirements, while existing GDPR rights and obligations remain in force (Art. 2(7)).

question: We use an AI tool to pre-screen applicants. Do we have to change anything tomorrow?
answer_points: An AI system intended to analyse and filter job applications is high-risk (Art. 6(2); Annex III, point 4(a)).
The high-risk obligations for Annex III systems apply from 2 December 2027, so they do not apply tomorrow (Art. 113(c)(i)).
The duty to take AI literacy measures already applies to providers and deployers (Art. 4(1); Art. 113(a)).
This is not legal advice; the specific use case requires individual legal review.

question: May we train our AI model on customer data we already hold?
answer_points: A legal basis is required, such as consent or legitimate interests (gdpr Art. 6(1)).
The data may not be further processed in a manner incompatible with the purposes for which it was collected (gdpr Art. 5(1)(b)).

Without consent or a legal provision for the new purpose, compatibility must be assessed, including the link between the purposes, the context of collection, the nature of the data, the consequences and the safeguards (gdpr Art. 6(4)).
This is not legal advice; the specific use case requires individual legal review.
